summary:
Santa Catarina stands under the national framework of Brazil, where same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013 under National Council of Justice Resolution 175/2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change, spousal and residence categories treat same-sex and opposite-sex couples identically, and a 2019 Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling (ADO 26) makes discrimination and hate crimes on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds punishable as equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989. A visitor's entry, documents and family status are therefore handled on the same footing as any other traveller's.

In one respect Santa Catarina runs worse than the rest of the country. It is the only Brazilian state to have enacted a statutory bathroom restriction, and it is the venue of a nationally decisive refusal: staff at a Florianópolis shopping centre barred a trans woman from the women's restroom, where she urinated on herself in front of shoppers and had to travel home by public transport. On 6 June 2024 the Supreme Federal Tribunal rejected her appeal, leaving such refusals lawful under ordinary private-premises rules. The concrete exposure a visibly trans visitor faces is in shops, restaurants and transport hubs across the state.

Foreign partners are protected in practice. A Florianópolis judge of the 1st Civil Court, M. C. F. Ribeiro da Silva, blocked immigration authorities from deporting an Italian citizen who had lived more than ten years in a stable relationship with a lesbian Brazilian. Foreign same-sex marriages are recognised for immigration purposes, including the spousal residence permit.

Florianópolis itself is named among Brazil's broadly welcoming major cities, with active LGBTQ+ communities, pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing same-sex marriages, adoptions and name or gender-marker changes. Smaller cities and rural parts of Santa Catarina may present more social friction, although legal rights are identical nationwide.

The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's March 2026 country overview records that LGBTIQ people in Brazil still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions, and guarantees apply equally to visitors in Santa Catarina.
tangentialFactors:
A deeply conservative Congress has produced a surge of anti-LGBTIQ legislative proposals, including efforts to repeal the marriage equality recognised by the Supreme Court in 2013. The guarantees a visitor relies on are therefore contested at the political level even while they remain in force.

Violence against LGBTI people elsewhere in Brazil illustrates the surrounding risk environment. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife; in the October 2024 municipal elections close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle.

Detention conditions elsewhere show the gap between rules and practice. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, requires judges to consult LGBTI detainees on their placement and prohibits using LGBTI-specific spaces as disciplinary isolation, yet a peer-reviewed census carried out between April and June 2021 in Rio de Janeiro state prisons interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates across eleven units operated as masculine, describing placement in male units as a double punishment.

Courts elsewhere have extended protection to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing.
localsOnly:
The Constitution of Santa Catarina contains an anti-discrimination clause dating to 2002 that lists sexual orientation among non-discrimination grounds; as of 2019 it does not address discrimination against transgender people.

Since 2020, people in Santa Catarina have obtained documents recording non-binary gender through the courts or notarial offices, although no specific state law prescribes this. The Superior Court of Justice has ruled that non-binary people may amend their civil registry to reflect their gender identity.

Residents have access to the full national suite of family and status rights: same-sex marriage under CNJ Resolution 175/2013, joint and second-parent adoption confirmed by Supreme Federal Tribunal case RE 846.102 (2015), and gender-marker changes without surgery.

In September 2025 the federal government reinstated the National LGBTI+ Health Technical Committee, a participatory mechanism dissolved in 2019, for shaping and monitoring inclusive public-health policy.

Lower courts have pressed the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, bringing trans people within the country's violence-prevention statutes.
outOfScopeNotes:
The full text and statutory basis of Santa Catarina's bathroom restriction, and which premises or buildings it binds, are not stated in the sources held for this record; the restriction is reported at the level of its existence and of the 6 June 2024 Supreme Federal Tribunal refusal.

Whether the 2002 non-discrimination clause of the Santa Catarina Constitution has ever been applied to a transgender claim, and how the state's courts treat trans-specific complaints, are unresolved on the available sources.

No Santa Catarina-specific figures on violence, hate-crime reporting or police handling against trans people are sourced here; the violence evidence in this record is national or comes from other states.

The status of trans detainees in Santa Catarina's own prison system, and whether National Council of Justice Resolution 348 and Resolution 366 are followed in the state's units, is not sourced. The only prison census available covers Rio de Janeiro state.

The statement that the state constitutional clause does not address transgender discrimination is dated as of 2019 and has not been re-verified against later amendments.
